Let me analyze each division's additional layer relative to parent.

Parent 0.35 — national framework: hostile document/entry regime, passport marker restrictions, X markers stopped, entry screening risk, trans athlete ban, plus facilities restrictions vary by state. National hate crime law covers gender identity; national employment protection. Custody harm documented. So parent at 0.35 (High Risk band, top of it).

Now each division:

Dossier 1: Virginia? State statute defining man/woman, facilities ban covering locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centers, dormitories, prisons; "Worst states" tier, one below Do Not Travel. Religious refusal statute, no statewide nondiscrimination, city ordinances, student-outing bill passed. No documented arrest under the facilities statute. So additional hostile layer: statewide facilities statute covering all those spaces — that's a tier-1 universal exposure (restrooms in public buildings). Rates below parent. Parent 0.35 → maybe 0.22-0.26. This is a "worst states" group one tier below DNT. I'd say 0.22.

Dossier 2: Florida? 2023 public-facility statute covering government-owned/leased buildings including airports, parks, beaches, schools; criminal trespass for refusing to leave; one documented arrest (activist, case dismissed on standing). Also driver's licence marker ban (Jan 2024), birth certificate closure. Travel advisory issued by LGBTQ orgs. Also a statistic: 3.7 trans women murdered per 100k per year — described as "near the top... labelled Do Not Travel" but the article's finding is that law severity doesn't correlate with killing rates. Hmm, 3.7 per 100k is quite high compared to general US murder rate ~6/100k... actually 3.7 per 100k for trans women is below the general homicide rate — background-level, per rule 16. So violence axis: near-baseline; don't elevate. The facility statute is the harshest: covers airports, beaches, parks — visitor-facing universal exposure with criminal penalty. That is the worst of the five. So lowest score. Maybe 0.18-0.20. Note the enforcement is documented (one arrest) but case dismissed. Still universal exposure with criminal trespass. I'd give 0.18.

Dossier 3: Illinois? Civil rights statute covering gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, credit (2020); hate crime law covers GI; panic defense repealed; X marker on licences; sodomy repealed; marriage equality; schools restrictions (2023 education dept bathroom/pronoun policy for students, intended reversal 2026); athletics ban Feb 2025; conversion therapy ban for minors. July 2026 risk assessment places it in low-risk group, youth-only policies unlikely to extend to adults. So this is above parent clearly. But the parent national framework (passport/entry) still applies. Score above 0.35. How much? The national entry/document exposure is a real traveler-facing risk (passport confiscation, entry refusal, X marker not processed, body scanners). That caps it. State adds protections. I'd say 0.50-0.55. Given parent is 0.35 and this state is protective in public accommodations, facilities, hate crimes — but the parent's entry regime is unavoidable. Maybe 0.50.

Dossier 4: Kentucky? 2023 statute overriding veto: school bathroom restriction for public school students + care ban for minors. Birth certificate requires surgery. 2022 trans girls school sports ban. No statewide facilities rule for adults. Hate crime excludes gender identity. 19 municipalities nondiscrimination ordinances. State employment EO. So mostly resident/youth-facing; adult visitor-facing exposure is limited to national layer. Additional negative: hate crime exclusion (resident-facing remedy gap, not visitor exposure per rule). School facility restriction doesn't apply to adult visitors. So this is roughly at or slightly above parent — but parent's facilities-restriction context: this state has no adult facility ban, so relative to the parent average (where many states have bans), it's a bit better. Weather: no documented trans-specific violence. I'd say 0.40-0.44. Compared with dossier 3, clearly lower.

Hmm, but rule 1: absence of resident-facing machinery is not a deduction but also not a credit. The state's protections (municipal ordinances, EO) are resident-facing. The main visitor-facing difference is absence of an adult facilities ban. Parent at 0.35 reflects the average including states with bans. So a state with no adult ban sits above parent average: maybe 0.42.

Dossier 5: Minnesota? Courts repeatedly block anti-trans laws; 2026 bill codifying biological definitions was passed and is being litigated (unresolved). Facilities law 2025 blocked by temporary restraining order (status unresolved). Care ban struck down. Documents: marker changes blocked since 2022 pending trial. So the enacted hostile statutes are enjoined. But: recent 2026 law signed 24 March 2026 codifying sex definitions across 60 sections including driver's licences and marriage licences; litigation pending, no ruling. Facilities law 2025 restrained but not permanently. Risk assessment improved standing — only state whose standing improved. Protective court record. Rule 11: functioning courts working FOR trans people = mitigation. So above parent, maybe higher than dossier 3? Dossier 3 has statutory protections in force; dossier 5 has hostile statutes enacted but enjoined — meaning the operative practice is protections via courts, but unresolved litigation creates uncertainty, and a newly signed 2026 law applies (not yet enjoined — plaintiffs moved to add to litigation, no ruling). Rule: unknown is not midpoint; the 2026 law is in force unless enjoined. That's a universal-exposure measure (driver's licence sex definition, applied across 60 sections) — but for a visitor, DL/marriage licence rules don't apply. Facilities law restrained. So visitor-facing: no active facility ban (restrained), no care ban, courts protective. I'd put dossier 5 around 0.48-0.50, similar to dossier 3, maybe slightly below because of pending litigation risk and unresolved 2026 law. Hmm.

Actually for a visitor, the state's 2026 law codifying sex definitions could reach anti-discrimination protections — it applies across anti-discrimination protections, which is resident-focused. And a stated hostility by legislature but courts blocking. I'd give 5: 0.47, 3: 0.52.

Let me reconsider dossier 3 vs 5. Dossier 3: statutory protections in force, hate crime covers GI, X marker, but has school bathroom/pronoun policies for students and an athletics ban — not visitor-facing. Low-risk group in assessment. Dossier 5: courts block; the assessment improved it but hostile statutes remain enacted. Dossier 5 also has religious refusal law (2021) granting right to discriminate — resident-facing service access could affect visitors (a business refusing service). That's a documented hostility channel. So I'd put 5 slightly below 3.

Now dossier 4: no adult facility ban, no statewide protections for adults outside national, hate crime excludes GI, religious freedom law 2013 allows refusals (service denial to trans visitors? "whether religious-exemption has been applied to transgender-specific service refusals is not sourced"). So open question, light. 0.42.

Dossier 1: statewide facility statute covering restrooms, lockers, shelters, dormitories, prisons — criminal? Not criminal; and no documented enforcement. Still tier-1 universal exposure. Also religious-refusal statute allowing service denial with qualified immunity. No nondiscrimination. "Worst states" tier one below DNT. Score maybe 0.25.

Dossier 2: facility statute with criminal trespass, covers airports, beaches, parks — broadest visitor contact, documented arrest. 0.19.

Let me finalize:
1: 0.25
2: 0.19
3: 0.51
4: 0.42
5: 0.47
